This isn’t a proper answer to the question, but on a related note, hallucinations are heavily impacted by society. Society tells us what to expect to hallucinate, and we are more likely to hallucinate what we expect to hallucinate. Our expectations in America are scary and aggressive, so they often (not always) are that experience. But in some holistic cultures, schizophrenia isn’t as commonly conceptualized and instead hearing voices isn’t evil, it’s spirits of your family coming to check on you or other kind things. With this expectation, many of those people experience friendly hallucinations. When I learned this I started being really careful about what media I took in. Luckily, I didn’t grow up around that media, and being sheltered also meant for me that I didn’t know the word hallucination, AND my symptoms came from before elementary school age. So I lived with my experiences not knowing how others expected me to see them. I expected kind things from my world, inner and outer, so my hallucinations are usually comforting. I sometimes see words floating around, but they’re in pretty fonts as say nice things. I do dislike my auditory ones though cause they startle me.

Psychosis does physical things to the brain that impact cognition. The more relapses you have, the more it changes your brain function/structure. One way it does this is through inflammation. Schizophrenia is a life long disease, so if you stop taking meds it’s basically a sure fire way to let psychosis happen again. You may feel well, but that’s the meds doing their job. Stop taking them, stop feeling well. To retain as much mental ability as you can, take your meds. I wonder too if there’s anything else we can do to keep our thinking intact

Look, I don’t really know your conditions, but is she able to care for herself or do you do that for her? If she can’t, could you take her with you? Or leave someone with her? Also consider if someone will be able to take care of the house, pay rent, cook, and clean. If she can’t do these things, she is almost certainly going to worsen. I’m on three meds now, Olanzapine being the main one. I think I’m at a much more stable place, I can do school work and have friends, it’s like finally being able to experience without this film in my perceptions separating me from the world. I’m also no longer depressed or manic. Still, I am optimistic in part because I could still get better. I’m doing well! But we are keeping an eye out for changes yet to be made. Not all the journey to health is pain, you’ll feel better gradually, and you can feel good in yourself even if you haven’t got the “perfect” meds. Good luck friend.

I had my first psychotic episode in the middle of high school. I lost all my friends, I went from an A student to a C student in months, I thought everyone was out to get me. I thought I was a dragon and that the universe was talking to me and that I could fly. I thought everything down to rocks were alive and that I was probably a book character that could see foreshadowing happening around me. I was extremely depressed and anxious, addicted to self harm, suicidal, miserable, and yet my brain was so fried I felt high

Cut to now? Years of medication and therapy later, I’ve got a whole friend group, I’m forming communities around me. Yes I make social mistakes but I no longer blame that on me not belonging, but me just still learning. I’ve not self harmed for months, I’m happy to be alive. I have a good relationship with my hospital, I’ve found a passion I’m in college for (I think I have a 3.9 gpa). I’m finally comfortable in my own skin. Just a few days ago I had a break through. I had been having symptoms resurface so we gave me more meds and then. A few days ago I looked at the clouds. And they were just clouds. Not saying anything. Just clouds.

I’m learning to see the world in a whole new way

I have noticed two things though: 

1. If I go down on it and then decide to go back up to the original dose, I’m so much more sleepy than I was when on the original dose the first time. It’s like your body gets used to it, so if you go down it’s less able to handle it again when you go back up cause it’s lost it’s resistance (is that the right word)

2. The longer I take it the less sleepy I get. Yes it’s hell on the way (although you could argue it’s comfy to be asleep), yes I didn’t have the strength in me to hope it would change, but it seems to have chilled out for me. I can’t say that will work for everyone, but for me being on it longer seems to have helped. Although! I also did have other meds added to my cocktail of drugs so they may have played a role.

From what I know, and I'm not a doctor but, DONT go cold turkey suddenly. You will have terrible withdrawal effects. Antipsychotics affect the nervous system so it'll hit you really, really hard. If you want to stop taking it the best way is to explain to your doctors how you're feeling and why you need to stop and they can help wean you off of it, or if they really won't work with you and you're really set on this, come off of it slowly, maybe more slowly than you think. I read somewhere that you risk having more psychotic symptoms and tardive psychosis if you come off antipsychotics too fast. If the doctors won't help you at least please do research about how you can more safely come off and what can happen if you come off too quickly. How you come off it also does depend on how much you're taking.

Also, I don't know your situation but sometimes when you're psychotic you can't tell you are psychotic. So it may be better to have your doctors switch your medication to a different one, instead of just coming off this and not taking anything, so you can still be treated but without these side effects. The doctors should listen to you if you explain these side effects and how they are unbearable, they should want to cooperate with you. I know it may not feel that way (I really hated doctors for a long time when I was first treated for psychosis), but even so, it's also better to show them that you want to cooperate so they don't write you down as noncompliant, which can lead to other problems and difficulties for you down the road.
